title: Linux Learning Station
user: A parent or teacher setting up an older shared Linux computer for 5–10-year-olds who needs offline, age-progressive learning activities without accounts.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent using GCompris for a five-year-old asks what comes next, saying free Linux educational games seem limited for older children.
A college Python instructor describes per-user installation as a classroom blocker and needs a ready-to-use environment for 50 students at login.

recurrence: Two independent classroom/home setup requests expose a deployment problem alongside the content gap. Severity is medium-high where accounts, app installs, and weak connectivity exclude devices from use.
current_workaround: Install assorted apps one by one, rely on browser sites, or default to GCompris past its intended level.
incumbents_and_gap: GCompris, TuxMath, and web learning sites exist, but discovery and age progression are fragmented. The gap is a single offline launch page with a small curated progression and no child account.
smallest_useful_product: Installable offline PWA with six original, local mini-activities (patterns, keyboarding, logic, spelling, number sense, creative drawing), parent-configured age bands, and printable progress code. Non-goals: a content marketplace, cloud profiles, and licensed game aggregation.
success_measure: In five home/classroom pilots, an adult can install and start a child activity in under five minutes without creating an account; children return for three sessions in one week.
monetization: one-time — schools and families can buy an offline bundle without tracking children or managing subscriptions.
constraints: COPPA/GDPR-K by design: no telemetry, chat, ads, or external links in child mode; original or permissively licensed assets only; work on low-end Chromium.
why_distinct: It solves local deployment and age progression with original micro-activities rather than cloning a commercial kids’ platform.
